```bash
root@controlplane:/etc/kubernetes$ sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -text | egrep 'Subject:|Issuer:|DNS:|IP Address:'
        Issuer: CN = kubernetes
        Subject: CN = kube-apiserver
                DNS:controlplane, DNS:kubernetes, DNS:kubernetes.default, DNS:kubernetes.default.svc, DNS:kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local, IP Address:10.96.0.1, IP Address:172.30.1.2
```

```bash
root@controlplane:/etc/kubernetes$ sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -noout -text | egrep 'Subject:|Issuer:'
sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -noout -text | egrep 'Subject:|Issuer:'
        Issuer: CN = kubernetes
        Subject: CN = kubernetes
```
Observation: admin.conf references the CA and a client cert/key from /etc/kubernetes/pki . This is how kubectl proves who you are to the API server.
```bash
root@controlplane:/etc/kubernetes$ sudo egrep -n 'certificate-authority|client-certificate|client-key' /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf
4:    certificate-authority-data: 
17:    client-certificate-data: 
18:    client-key-data: 
```
```bash
root@controlplane:/etc/kubernetes$ sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-etcd-client.crt -noout -text | egrep 'Subject:|Issuer:|DNS:|IP Address:'
        Issuer: CN = etcd-ca
        Subject: CN = kube-apiserver-etcd-client
```
```bash
root@controlplane:/etc/kubernetes$ sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver-kubelet-client.crt -noout -text | egrep 'Subject:|Issuer:|DNS:|IP Address:'
        Issuer: CN = kubernetes
        Subject: O = kubeadm:cluster-admins, CN = kube-apiserver-kubelet-client
```
